## The five analysts of the robustness study {#the-five-published-analysts}

Before you begin, here is what the five analysts found when they reanalysed the same claim, as recorded in the robustness study:

| Analyst | Tool | Statistic | N | Partial r, recorded | Reproduced in the exercise |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 018OL | R | t = −1.21 | 420 | −0.060 | yes, on its 420 cells |
| C6HJR | R | t = −3.80 | 270 | −0.242 | yes, on the course panel |
| KEVF1 | R | t = −5.90 | 209,826 | −0.452 | no – needs the respondent files |
| KQXUE | Stata | t = −7.17 | 270 | −0.419 | yes, on its 270 country-years |
| PRL47 | Stata | z = −3.59 | 394,575 | −0.006 | no – needs the respondent files |

All five reported a negative effect, in the direction of the original. The recorded partial correlations range from −0.006 to −0.452, a factor of nearly 80, but most of that spread comes from the conversion of each test statistic into a correlation rather than from the analyses themselves. PRL47 and C6HJR report almost the same statistic, yet the z of PRL47 was converted on the number of respondents, which pulls any correlation towards zero. Section 4 of the [background page](../../cases/europeanisation/index.qmd#sec-recorded) shows how the conversion works, and the [reference marks](../../cases/europeanisation/curve.qmd#reference-marks) of the specification curve place each result on the degrees of freedom of its own inference.
